slides.title: Surviving stereocilia can repair local actin damage
body: Wagner and colleagues examined gaps in the actin cores of mouse auditory stereocilia after traumatic noise exposure. An actin core contains many bundled filaments that help maintain the projection’s shape. A local gap can weaken this framework while leaving the surrounding stereocilium and its hair cell alive.

The gaps were largely repaired within a week through incorporation of newly synthesized actin. XIRP2 contributed to recruitment of actin at damaged regions, and loss of its normal function impaired the repair process. Repair of a damaged projection therefore uses new structural material within an existing sensory receptor.

The accompanying fibroblast recording tests full-length XIRP2 after a laser-induced stress-fiber lesion. Unlike the isolated C-terminal domain shown earlier, this tagged full-length construct was not recruited to those sites under the tested conditions. Different protein constructs and cellular environments can expose different parts of a proposed damage-recognition mechanism.

slides.title: Repairing a bundle preserves an existing receptor
body: Actin-core repair, tip-link recovery, and replacement of a dead hair cell are distinct biological processes. A surviving cell retains its membrane, much of its bundle, and potentially its neural connections. Local repair can restore a damaged part without rebuilding the entire sensory receptor and its place within the epithelium.

The XIRP2 study examined sublethal bundle injury and found a force-sensitive protein region that could accumulate at strained actin structures. The study also measured auditory stereocilia directly after noise exposure. These two preparations address complementary questions about recognizing damage and replacing the structural material lost from the bundle.

A temporary recovery of hearing sensitivity can therefore occur without producing new hair cells. Restored ion balance, recovering transduction machinery, or repaired bundle structure can each improve a surviving receptor’s function. Establishing regeneration requires evidence that new sensory cells appeared, rather than inferring their production solely from an improved threshold.

slides.title: Some animals replace damaged sensory hair cells
body: **Hair-cell regeneration** means producing replacement sensory cells after existing cells die. Birds can replace damaged auditory hair cells, and zebrafish replace hair cells in their lateral-line organs. The lateral line detects water movement along the body; its regeneration provides a comparative model rather than direct evidence of restored hearing.

The replacement cells can arise from **supporting cells**, neighboring cells that help maintain the sensory tissue. In small zebrafish **neuromasts**, the lateral-line sensory organs, supporting cells divide to produce new hair cells. Other supporting cells replenish the progenitor population, allowing the organ to retain cells capable of responding to another injury.

Thomas and colleagues labeled different supporting-cell populations and followed their descendants during regeneration. The populations differed in how readily they generated hair cells. Removing selected supporting cells reduced subsequent hair-cell replacement, showing that regeneration depends on which surviving cells remain available to rebuild the sensory organ.

slides.title: Replacement cells must rebuild an organized sensory organ
body: A new hair cell must occupy a useful position within the sensory organ. Its bundle also needs the appropriate **polarity**, the orientation that determines which direction of movement excites it. Producing additional cells without restoring their arrangement can leave the tissue unable to represent the original mechanical stimulus correctly.

Viader-Llargués and colleagues followed individual cells as zebrafish neuromasts recovered from partial injury. Live imaging revealed cell divisions, changes in cell identity, and movement within the repairing organ. The regenerated tissue recovered its characteristic organization, proportions of cell types, and hair-cell polarity after the experimental damage.

Completely removing a neuromast did not produce the same recovery as leaving surviving tissue. The remaining cells provide both a source of replacement cells and a local environment in which the organ can rebuild. A regenerative response therefore depends on the tissue that survives the injury, including its supporting-cell populations.

slides.title: Adult mouse supporting cells can acquire hair-cell traits
body: Adult mammalian cochleae do not normally replace lost hair cells effectively. Researchers therefore try to change the identity of surviving supporting cells. **Transcription factors** are proteins that regulate gene activity; experimentally supplying selected factors can activate parts of the developmental program that originally produced a sensory hair cell.

Sun and colleagues supplied **ATOH1 and IKZF2** together in adult mouse cochlear supporting cells. Some cells acquired outer-hair-cell-like characteristics and expressed **prestin**, the motor protein responsible for outer hair cell length changes. Damaging the original outer hair cells increased the efficiency of this experimentally induced conversion.

Expression of prestin identifies an important step toward an outer hair cell identity. Restoring cochlear amplification also requires a correctly organized bundle, appropriate electrical responses, and mechanical coupling to the surrounding tissue. The reported cell conversion did not establish restoration of normal hearing in an adult mammal.

slides.title: Maturation makes the hair-cell program harder to restart
body: Young cochlear cells respond more readily to attempts at reprogramming than older cells. One reason concerns **chromatin**, the DNA and associated proteins that package genetic information. A transcription factor can activate a gene more readily when the relevant DNA region remains accessible within that cellular packaging.

Iyer and colleagues compared ATOH1 alone with combinations including **GFI1 and POU4F3** in mice. Reprogramming soon after birth produced many hair-cell-like cells. When induction began one week later, all three factors were needed for effective conversion, and the resulting cells showed less mature characteristics than those induced earlier.

The investigators measured gene expression and DNA accessibility in individual cells. Hair-cell gene regions became less accessible with age, while communication between neighboring cells, including **Notch signaling**, also restricted conversion. Changing a cell’s identity therefore requires overcoming both its internal gene-regulation state and signals from surrounding tissue.

slides.title: Repairing cochlear synapses differs from replacing cells
body: Noise can damage the connections between inner hair cells and auditory nerve fibers even when the hair cells survive. These connections contain **ribbon synapses**, specialized release sites that support rapid glutamate transmission. Rebuilding a damaged synapse addresses a different injury from replacing a dead sensory receptor cell.

Wan and colleagues increased **neurotrophin-3**, a locally acting protein supplied by cochlear supporting cells, in mice. Following acoustic trauma, the manipulation promoted recovery of ribbon synapses and cochlear neural responses. The experiment examined repair around surviving hair cells rather than conversion of supporting cells into replacement hair cells.

A larger auditory nerve response can reflect improved transmission from the receptor to the nerve. It does not require that new receptor cells have appeared. Counting hair cells, examining synaptic contacts, and measuring neural responses therefore answer separate questions about which peripheral structures were damaged and which structures recovered.

slides.title: Restored hearing requires working cells and connections
body: A replacement inner hair cell must convert bundle movement into a graded voltage change and release transmitter onto auditory nerve fibers. A replacement outer hair cell must contribute mechanical amplification. These different functions mean that producing a cell with a hair-cell marker is an early milestone rather than a complete hearing treatment.

Translation to people requires delivering a treatment to the appropriate cochlear cells while preserving the surrounding sensory tissue. New cells must survive, develop correctly oriented bundles, and acquire the properties needed at their location along the cochlea. Inner hair cells also need functional synapses with surviving auditory nerve fibers.

Animal studies can test progressively stronger outcomes: cell identity, bundle structure, mechanical or electrical responses, synaptic transmission, and hearing-related performance. Evidence of recovery in one injury model does not establish recovery after every cause of deafness. Human treatment claims require clinical evidence demonstrating useful and sustained hearing improvement.

chapter_scope: Peripheral auditory system only. No cochlear nucleus, brainstem auditory circuits, thalamus, auditory cortex, or binaural computation. Comparative lateral-line and utricular examples are explicitly identified.

takeaways.cite: Carlson & Birkett (2022); primary studies in notes
refs: Carlson NR, Birkett MA (2022). Physiology of Behavior, Global Edition. 13th ed. Pearson. ISBN 9781292430256. Chapter 7, peripheral auditory material, printed pp. 193–197 and selected cochlear coding material pp. 200–202. Central pathways and localization excluded. Mature cochlear hair cells have graded receptor potentials; auditory nerve fibers generate spikes.

items.text: Outer- and middle-ear mechanics deliver pressure to the cochlea, where relative motion bends stereocilia and opens mechanically sensitive ion channels.
Prestin converts receptor voltage into force, improving sensitivity and frequency selectivity; inner hair cells supply most afferent sensory output.

items.lead: The nerve code has several dimensions.
items.text: Cochlear place, firing rate, and phase-locked timing provide different information. Phase locking does not require a spike on every sound cycle.
Calcium channels, ribbon organization, vesicle replenishment, and neuronal excitability determine how a graded receptor response becomes reliable nerve signaling.
Conductive defects, bundle injury, cell loss, synaptopathy, and neural loss require different measurements and different repair strategies.
Animal studies demonstrate replacement or repair under defined conditions. Human hearing restoration requires working receptors, appropriate connections, durable function, and clinical evidence.
